text: read the first chapter on Beautiful Testing. Should probably show that to my boss, she was just explaining my weird sense of humour...
Preparing a new course (in finnish) on acceptance testing. Should get the materials published with creative commons attribution next week.
Nice test managers session on agreements and organizing testing held today. More people could join in online monthly.
Summarizing recent lessons learned on acceptance testing (in the traditional sense). Core seems to be the difference of project vs. test mgr
Can top-down test improvement ever work? I have my doubts.
How little a portion of effort could I dare to dream for acceptance testing... I'm thinking 1 rather than 10 percent.
Just don't get it. Why some people insist semi-automation isn't automation. Great examples of useful things to share hiding there.
Continued thinking: is it possible to avoid test process improvement in a real-life test project? I can't manage.
When people say we should do a better plan, they seem to be saying that they need time for learning and thinking.
If one get paid more for "planning" testing = documenting than testing, exploratory testing may have difficulties.
As a tester, I should really not be bothered with costs of what we're testing. Leaves more time for the real stuff.
There's the popular notion of rather rebuilding than fixing at some point of badness of quality. How to recognize that point?
Wondering what definition of "requirements" would result in better testing in software project business...
@QAHatesYou In some places, you spend your days working on requirements instead of working code for years - and still don't get it right.
V-model confusion: system test without an end-to-end system even though one is available. System 0 organizational responsibility.
Drifting with meetings - need to take action to make progress instead of just being busy. Why was is seemingly easier with agile...
Promised to organize a discussion session (in Finnish) for test data related problems and solutions with data-intensive systems. Next:date.
Another question on testing-related dissertations. Should really do the list of who's working on what within testing research in Finland.
Looked at a group designing documented test cases. Nice cases, but would miss the bugs that are still there, and check same and devs did.
Theme: regression testing. Results get blocked with the idea of being safe by executing someone else's plan / my old plan.
How common can it really be to not be allowed to find bugs that don't jump at you from a spec. Can't be product vs. project business thing.
Should I keep concepts "test case" and "charter" more separate. Can't decide. Then my test design would get renamed to charter design.
Test case: detailed action (a test) or documentation. Still, my documented test cases are more of a collections of checklists.
Torn between local and global participation. Local testing community = Finnish language. Tried doing materials in both, won't work.
Ream I.M. Testy blog comments on exploratory testing. Should blog on how we scaled ET at my previous work place.
Should exploratory testing really be compared to static code analysis in efficiency? Like comparing apples and oranges.
Surprised my colleagues seemed to think exploratory testing requires UI. There's plenty of other interfaces to start with.
Difference in testing skills at my two places of work: not relevant. Comparing to subcontractor's skills in this area, old colleagues win.
ET: Not the documentation overhead being smaller, but the documentation rework being smaller.
@TuulaP Worry not, it went well.
Decided I'll do a series of ET sessions (in Finnish). Probably would start with addressing repeatability or collecting topics.
A day of reflection: I don't want to feel we did not make enough progress in testing after next 6 months. No excuses.
Too much planning, too little doing the actual thing. Is there options other than wait for traditional acceptance testing...
Doing my presentation on managing exploratory testing. Should have that ready during weekend, and could do an online run of it.
Nice idea #WeekendTesting, but the name... Around here practicing testing skills could happen during weekdays.
Again torn between two languages when writing about stuff. There's a lot of material already in English, but little in Finnish.
Finally recovering stuff since my harddrive breaking. Materials about to be uploaded to my testauskirja.com -site - in Finnish.
Today's theme was refining issue management process - yet another one. It's really not so difficult...
Very little value in "independent testing" if the tester is stricktly bound to the written requirements. Weird mantra taught to customers.
Need to think about logs this weekend. Would prefer ones that are helpful. :)
Keep thinking about customer - contractor relationship and testing. Sometimes more cost because of the responsibility barriers.
Why was it again that I should not wait with testing the whole until the pieces are finished? Less effort for testing if less open issues.
Promised to talk on testing + agile in customer perspective. Need to think what I'd do, don't really live agile as of now.
Why it is common to have test manager responsible for bug fix coordination, not just getting bugs listed with info. No time for testing.
@MauravdL Fairly small project with project and test manager. I can't get why the release manager role should not be PMs.
@MauravdL For me personally, not taking the responsibility is possible. Enough weight on what I say. Not same for all colleagues.
@MauravdL You're kind of writing the thing I'm thinking of. Then again, process fix won't be that easy. Customer - Contractor relationship.
Should update my materials on test documentation. Maybe tomorrow...
Defined a new course on test design lessons learned on pension insurance sector. Great way of thinking how my thinking changes.
Excellent test cases to support acceptance testing were done today. Great colleagues, wouldn't dare to call them non-testers.
A review meeting of request-reply message tests. A non-techie tester identified 6 unreported bugs in 15 minutes. Domain knowledge in action.
Reflecting on a book that was emphasizing SDET (software development engineer in test) over testing specialist. Context is so diffent.
Wondering what's the point in a testers career when "test all" changes to "test what brings value". Explaining why not test a change !=easy.
Would help if test environment was in our control. Why would that be impossible just for the sake of integrating to somebody else's sw?
Where I work, its relevant to remind people on negative tests = testing of error handling - not in written spec. Context customer acceptance
Its also relevant to tell them to try actual use instead of documented use. Especially if documented = pseudocoded.
My dislike of documentation has grown in the last year. Useful would be nice, blame / cost focusing is not.
@jamesmarcusbach Difference I see is in the willingness of testers to realize such functionality should exist. "Negative" = word to remind.
I've learned a lot thinking, explaining and comparing the meanings of words. There's a lot of hidden info there.
Seems to be much easier to list details that should be included when testing than putting them together in scenarios that you actually test.
@jamesmarcusbach I would expect there to be other non-positive testing than just error handling - anything unexpected, not just error msgs.
Why there's so little examples available on the choices of test case documentation people have made. Not singles, but "coverage".
@jamesmarcusbach Example I was thinking is use of two features in combination that should be allowed, but not mentioned in docs.
@jamesmarcusbach Would seem more clear to say error handling tests / combination tests / non-confirmatory tests since those are meant.
Heh, I wish there was some error handling to test in one of the current target systems... Error handling = "other system's concern" w/ API.
@jamesmarcusbach Thinking is the other way around: is there any form of negative testing on a system that has no error handling?
Wondering why some of my current colleagues - quite skilled in testing - prefer to not be called testers - work is reqs and acceptance.
@jamesmarcusbach I'm still under the impression that classically negative testing is some mixture of error handling and non-confirmatory.
@jamesmarcusbach But with thinking of how and why we use it at work, other words would describe the intent better.
Reading TPI Next today. Don't expect much of it...
@jamesmarcusbach confirmatory is the word I use on what you seem to have called checking lately. Or pretty close at least.
@jamesmarcusbach In my current sector, there is a lot of documentation worship. Anything that is not unambiguous --> customer pays more.
Theme next week: how to teach testing to people who do it and need to gain more skills, but want to say they are not testing.
@michaelbolton I get that there's more to checking than I could put in my 140 chars.
Frustrated with test case documentation. So many "it depends" details on which part could change. Really all I need is the test data.
@jamesmarcusbach Won't stop, as I did not start. Thinking through balance - I have 30 day test time at end of 2 yr project, with ~15 ppl.
@jamesmarcusbach with the project I work with it takes 2 days to find one set of test data that represents production data.
@jamesmarcusbach I'm thinking (for now) to direct planning just towards test data. Test cases are already title checklists.
Should think of coverage-widening examples like FreeMind search-and-repl. requirements-oriented testing exercise I've been running lately.
@michaelbolton Subcontractor is testing within their project. For the business specialist, preparation is happening.
@michaelbolton It would be crazy to make detailed plans two years in future, agreed. Some may try it, I won't.
@michaelbolton I'm working on changing the rules so that test execution would actually have both business and technical detail in use.
@michaelbolton I was told for years that the exploratory testing we did at my previous place "could not be done" in the current sector.
Time to write an acceptance test plan. 2 * A4 is my set goal - one for each project.
Run a test on another project to feel less management-oriented. Found a bug. Not looking forward to discussing "not bug, new requirement"
A comment from a project manager today´: planning their acceptance testing has been the most difficult project plan he has ever done.
Met an ex-colleague. She's losing interest in the field for managers pushing too much automation as agile guru's tell them.
Need to find a way of explaining that I could, just as the pm could, run a ccb and analyze all bugs - but would have less time listing them.
Again discussing duplicate bugs: duplicate of same symptoms in same place vs. as in same fix for both. My testers can't tell the latter.
@lanettecream On reporting bugs, usually avoid duplicates. Two organizations, one having tester-oriented and other dev-oriented definition.
@lanettecream Current organization I work with pushes responsibility of checking if duplicate report was duplicate on the tester.
@lanettecream It matters, since there's so little time to do testing. Checking if sth marked duplicate really was that is with the testers.
@lanettecream My problem is duplicate bookkeeping, that takes unnecessary energy without much value. And who should do it depends on org.
@lanettecream I start with the assumption that I have 1 day a week of business specialist as tester. Different context.
@lanettecream I still think there's many ways of defining "the job". Delegating may sometimes be possible, yet difficult here now.
@lanettecream If "the job" is time-boxed, what's the best use of the little time of the available skills.
@lanettecream Delegating is not dumping. Taking all just since its part of the job can easily lead to not testing. Sometimes I'd do it.
Amazing how much people are willing to pay for useless documentation. One of our rounds is useless - good evidence to avoid that in scale.
@QAHatesYou My experience is the opposite but the cost is hidden. Little value, lots of documentation.
There's something wrong in test improvement projects. Too many are set up on external assumption of testing being "bad" when it's not.
Interesting concept: test sth but w/ specialist skill, no budget available. Someone could just do it with somebody else's budget?
Need better examples of SOA test cases. Can't be 1 test = 1 XML message, it's just not that straighforward.
Tomorrow I have a half-day session to plan planning. Sometimes I can't help but laugh. Just get sth done for a change...
Got two replies on organizing a seminar day on testing in the banking / insurance sectors. Hoping for some real insight.
Discussed Quality Center at work again. What's this with "excel is really not an option" - won't take it that easily.
RT @jbtestpilot: Kaner: "People who push commodity view of testing are a cause of the *treatment* of testers as commodities by execs sol ...
@lanettecream wiki is an option. excel is better option, since it counts and colors the cells automatically and adds visual status info.
@lanettecream read your blog and was wondering how close your new context of testing is to mine. we have different ppl.
@lanettecream I've seen a lot of different ways of using QC, and I'm not comfortable with any of them. Used it often though.
I think we use Quality Center so that the One Responsible would be able to see all tests planned & run. He never looks though, but could...
Today I changed our tests to backlog mode. Less waste and wishful thinking. Metrics can be somewhat more brutal, yet realistic.
Shocking realization: very few test plans I've written or used were actually useful at all.
Test case review today. Lesson: too easy to go into too much detail and not trust at all "those who tested before me".
@workroomprds Sometimes the planning was useful, sometimes not. Some plans (with decent planning) ended up only meaningless, others bad.
I believe in agile style planning. Keep thinking of "last responsible moment to decide" and level of detail in time horizons.
Inspired from new coworker's comments. Majority of testing he's seen has been considered just buffer. I claim were not, am I in denial...
Another angle: the organization lost nothing by using the testing "phase" as buffer. More problems with way they see testing.
A little victory today. A project manager got a decision made that I've been trying to push for ages. Team power is great.
When assessing the start of customer acceptance test, what is reasonable to expect with regards to quality? What if my expectation is off?
@lanettecream I'm part of "the customer" nowadays. I get to decide. I just want to be reasonable.
I expect quality could be closer to what we had at my previous place of work before customer acceptance. Product vs. project business...
@lanettecream And it's really not up to customer, if it's defined in a contact. Unless you're willing to pay more. Perhaps should pay more.
@lanettecream I wish I could type. I mean contract, not contact. You're lucky if you don't have to deal with that part - contracts that is.
@lanettecream My role is being a test manager with good-enough networks to actually change things.
@lanettecream And whatever is out of contract, always cost more. I don't really believe in fixed-cost contracts, does not exist.
Need to wrap up my presentation on testing in multi-subcontractor projects. Little on testing, much of other that causes problems to testing
Tried again introducing concept of best-before dates for tests run. Seems it goes well to explain need to repeat tests.
Living the implications of separating requirements and testing. The reqs end up as system that does not work. Incremental lifecycle, please.
Discussed two used approaches on designing our tests today. In one we start with test data (needed for coverage) and in other requirements.
Need a positive approach to get away from being trained (again) as project manager when I just want to be a tester. Saying no will not work.
Lost track again: why is testing so difficult that a project manager can't get it organized with good testers... They're able, not willing?
I'm hoping #weekendtesting would happen sometime during work week. Weekends are reserved for family. Rename needed?
Can't overcome my crisis with differences of project and test manager. Managing expert testers does not need test emphasis in mgmt.
Local testing seminar today. Hope there's sth about testing, not just the frame into which testing must be placed.
I'm liking limit-tests-in-progress test design. Too easy to come up with ideas that take the bandwith, little completed.
One case of smart testing that I felt proud of today in local testing seminar. We're building a great testing community in Finland.
Next: build a retraining program for unemployed but potential becoming testers. Will start with two skills: see a bug and report a bug.
I really need to set up a local face-to-face forum to discuss doing testing, not just the frame into which we place testing. Need more time.
Somewhat useful test plan today. Somewhat large audience left the review with more of a common ground. None will look at the paper anymore.
I don't manage to keep up with my mails or blog but there' always time for a short sentence in twitter.
Agreed with my manager I get to go to CAST next year if I do my part and share some lessons. Trying not to miss the deadline this time...
@workroomprds Getting back to the idea I threw at you when we saw briefly in Finland. We should have get-together for ppl teaching ET.
Team session on understanding personalities prepared, with a testing twist. Should still work on SAP acceptance testing materials.
When the cost of a test environment is big enough, what would I actually need for getting our testing done... So many variables.
What's the deal with using production data in test environment or not? Thinking through options and implications.
About to try change an extremely script-oriented testing to exploratory in the next few hours.
Hours --> Days --> Years. Will see. Lots of coverage-related discussions coming up on using exploratory testing where it's not so usual.
Really excited to get to test a system that has 20+ years of history. The UI is actually rather handy when you get started.
Really interesting discussions on whether to invest in testing or not. There's sides of testing that go unnoticed by management.
A non-technical content specialist could test with XML messages. Can specify but can't see the result is as intended? How could that work...
Another rant: what's a _test_ manager who has 20+ years of experience being a project manager and 2 with test. Disliking the term test mgr.
I should find time to write about latest kanban-inspired test case design approach. We limit the number of tests in process at once.
@testobsessed Lots of people in Finland have asked for a Finnish version of your cheat sheet. Would it be ok for you if I did that?
Need to wrap up some materials on testing in insurance pension sector. Wondering what was special that has anything to do with testing...
Latest course feedback was 4,3 / 5. I liked one comment saying it was her first course that taught testing hands-on.
Again thinking through test cases and people thinking that they're doing good work following the written step-by-step instructions.
Looking forward to making a positive case on how to invest in test documentation in insurance pension sector. Is change possible, will see.
Experiencing the ups and downs with test plans. Today was definite down. After giving detailed comments, a PM suggest to narrow them down.
Inspired by team-building evening. Skipped a day of project management to feel a little more like a tester. Next week: scope my role.
Read a project plan from "testing perspective". Why won't they just put the project and test plans together and make a plan for the whole?
Seriously feeling "testing perspective" reading means think while you read. Need to work on shared reading techniques.
A colleague said its easy to show examples of what a good test case looks like. I live in parallel universe, hasn't been easy for years...
Amazingly easy view of what testing is when some testers expect the requirements analyst is responsible for telling them what to test.
Submitted some material to suggest doing things differently for our testing than current sector. Positive feeling about doing test smarter.
And yet another example today of test cases gone bad with Quality Center misguiding the thinking... Fixed already though.
@aritanninen My recent non-favorite is that test case design is priced higher than the execution. Whoever did that contract has no clue...
Another experience of clueless test manager trying to manage contents he does not quite understand... Why not let the testers do the work.
Great certification scheme by @michaelbolton: "I test. You observe. We talk. You decide."
I need certification scheme to certify managers capable of giving their testers enough space to do the work.
Whenever I work with test managers who don't manage to manage at all, I wonder if I'm lost on the management side completely...
Great discussion with yet another colleague in testing. Wishing there was some good way of translating "sapient testing" to Finnish.
The way I think of testing annoyes some process / method -oriented colleagues. There's never a final answer, and plans won't hold.
Great management in my place of work, providing support in doing testing with exploratory and different documentation than standard.
Should get my head straight on what to adress in 1-day training on customers guiding contractors from test perspective. Difficult.
Doing AST BBST next month. Thinking to promote that as an alternative to ISTQB. Would eventually need a Finnish version, though.
MBTI again in discussions. I was typed ENFP. I remember material from 2003 by Ross Collard, stating typical tester would be ISTJ.
Performance testing considerations today. Someone needs to remind me why would I want to use the expensive tools when there's free ones.
@jbtestpilot Quite a wide selection of open-source tools. I just feel frustrated with LoadRunner for a change.
Thinking through complex server system dates and impact to testing. I need to draw a picture to understand this.
Thinking why one of our acceptance testers wants stepwise tests, while others are comfortable exploring. First reason stated: interruptions
Trying again to explain the tasks of test manager vs. project manager. There's some difference difficult to grasp at my work.
Some news of support for my traditional to exploratory -change. Next weeks will show if I get the chance to do things bit differently.
Personal accomplishment: found and logged a bug today, still not all lost on management side. Will never give up on testing hands-on.
Changed from product business to pension insurance to show exploratory testing is possible there. Made significant progress today.
No peers nearby introducing exploratory into highly plan- and document driven industry. Would be nice to talk with ppl in same situation.
RT @tkiuru: Testing Dojo in Helsinki 10th Nov http://bit.ly/aoZQb6
@ThomasPonnet Same thing on software-testing -list on yahoo. Would still like some local peers as well.
Sector-wise not ready for exploratory testing. Will do in one company only. At least they know we'll talk again in 8 months...
Found my third bug on the text message system for ordering taxis here. Was told my by driver my problems cannot happen for real.
We'll have an exploratory testing session within weeks. I'd hope to know the app beforehand, ET should not be seen as way for the unprepared
Asked my project manager if I can rewrite the accepted test plan that is correct but useless. Feels great to throw that out, have learn lot.
Remembered facilitation is being lazy, stupid and slow: not doing things for others, asking questions and letting others think themselves.
I don't like test improvement programs. They tend to get resourced with mgrs suggesting unnecessary controls. I'm for small scale in impr.
Need to take time on listing essential skills in testing as we know it for the roles we have. When title says testing, it does not mean that
Need to work on test environments in a case where you can't have as much as you like. What is enough and how to decide...
I'm new to mainframe testing, so in a weird way I enjoyed running into my first abend yesterday. Never thought of the terminology difference
@teemuvesala If you think you have common vocabulary because of the certificate, you're off a bit. You may have a common reference to one...
@teemuvesala Just had an argument with one of our subcontractors reps on them using "the standard V-model". Sales pitch gone bad.
Thinking about the need to test with future dates. Is it more of a habit than an actual need in almost every project...
Thanks to @tkiuru, a nice testing dojo and one more experience for myself for participating. More testing experience in the room next time?
What would be the most relevant testing topics for the financial sector. Need to decide this weekend for a local session.
Testing dojo was mostly about observing. Weekend testing seems more active. What should I call active session on during workweek?
SOA testing mini-seminar in Helsinki 13.1.2010, 15 - 18 for Finnish Association for Software Testing. Date set, one more presenter to go.
@plyytinen Have you thought about advertising the testing dojo? Or what kind of skills you'd like to see in the room to learn from?
@plyytinen With 12 slots, you can have hopes for different types of participants and would advertise to different audiences.
Summarized on two slides what is essentially different in pension insurance sector testing. I like what I learned for now. More tomorrow.
First lesson on the AST BBST course done. Somewhat fun, somewhat isolated. Looking for new depths in the material.
Interesting personal lesson today. Business people would rather have test data "from production" than change it intentionally for testing.
@can_test These business people are my test team, but not the only test team. So I'm thinking also sharing responsibities between the two.
AST BBST Foundation Lesson 4 to continue now. Course has reminded me both why I dislike and like groupwork.
Almost done with BBST Foundation course. Next to find out how badly I answered the exam and do the grading part. Can't avoid feedback.
Workwise recent themes of learnings: test environments, test data, contracts and testing, incluencing contractors, misuse of QC ... Lots!
When partially responsible for a potentially really bad test plan, what to do. Fix or let the others worry about it...
I'm doing my first presentation on January where I show QC in my use - in somewhat unusual way. Still would prefer excel.
I worry about a style of handpicking test data to match a specification. Could it be possible they are NOT missing anything relevant?
@jamesmarcusbach business specialists wrote a specification on a data-intensive system and are supposed to test for acceptance.
@jamesmarcusbach ...so for each thing they think they change, they select specific case in database, ignoring anything they don't think of.
@aritanninen I'm sure no, I tested. My uninformed brute-force selection of test data reveals problems. Future shows if they were missed.
@jamesmarcusbach @michaelbolton I like the term "demonstration magic". Describes this better than checking vs. testing.
@jamesmarcusbach Thinking overoptimistically in a different way: since there's many customers, maybe we don't have to do the hard work.
Today after 16 months of testing work in a new company, first acceptance test  completed. Years of planning and preparation, crazy.
Amused with the idea of checking vs. testing when most of my testing life is planning and getting ready. Interesting context this one...
I need to think of examples of bugs that a professional tester without domain knowledge can be expected to find in pension insurance sector.
Having thought about ít, I don't particularly appreciate the form we had in Helsinki Testing Dojo. The one in tampere will be a workshop.
@jbtestpilot Too bad for CFP on CAST this year. At least trying to contribute was an agreed part of me getting there.
"... your contact information from one of their Member Board representatives as an individual who might be a detractor of the ISTQB scheme"
Still wondering if I have the energy to answer five questions on why I might be a detractor...
@jbtestpilot some U.S marketing firm contracted by ISTQB to conduct research for the organization. My name is on the foundation syllabus.
@jamesmarcusbach apparently I've been names a detractor for being asked the questions. I tried it, wasted my time, won't do that again.
Interesting how difficult it is to say you're learning while testing in my current project. People are supposed to know already. I don't.
Doing a presentation on data-driven testing in comparison to spec-driven. Trying to dispel the idea that test design excludes execution.
Interesting how people turn failures to successes. For a bad performance system, showing what we already knew is not a successful test.
No wonder we lose opportunities for testing when the times we get the chance we fail the business information need and claim success.
Reading requirements from customer to contractor that requires testing to happen by someone else than the programmer. Bad thing to ask.
Having problems with the idea of doing acceptance testing on an old build just because old is safe and new has risks. The new one goes live!
Huge gap between continuous / regular integration in previous workplace vs. current idea of avoiding must-have changes for months.
Why would I believe 224 pieces of data (ppl with complex histories) would be enough coverage for a system that handles millions of people?
I'm building a case against spec based testing and hand-picking data to match that specification. I don't believe it can work.
@mgaertne You would not happen to know how a tester thinking of relocating to Germany would find potential places - any sites for that?
RT @niittyviita: Sehän on vain järkevää perustaa kriittiset järjestelmät epävakaille käyttöjärjestelmille: http://bit.ly/i04fdw #in #tes ...
Anyone know any good material on test data -related issues in data warehousing systems? I must be looking in all the wrong places.
Time of scorecard creation at work. High anxiety, I can't stick to my decision of not to care about the whole thing.
RT @AST_News: #CAST2011 Program Announced! http://bit.ly/hNi5zR See you in Seattle, WA in Aug 8-11 #softwaretesting #qa #testing ^BY
Not having enough time to help everyone at work makes me feel like I'm not a team player. I like to have time to test, not just talk of it.
Testing dojo #2 next week in Helsinki. I should contact some colleagues in Tampere to get one organized there in May.
Lucky number 13, the amount of bugs we had time to log today. Week-old bug in investigation on whether there's ways around it. Love testing.
I miss working with testing people who find challenging their ideas fun, not as cause of fear. Getting culture in place with some groups...
RT @plyytinen: HOX! One slot available in #TestingDojo II, Helsinki today due to cancellations. Bang the drum and let's get that slot fi ...
Yet another discussion of excel vs. quality center. I still prefer the first. Added dislike for lost tests for delete accidents recently.
Testing Dojo over and done with, thanks to @plyytinen for organizing. Have some ideas of things I'd want to try on how to learn from others.
@aritanninen Laittamalla viestin postituslistalle, sytyke-testaus-kerho@pcuf.fi. Sinä vai minä, molemmat käy :)
Now we don't test enough since we have less hours used for the results. This should be interesting...
@aritanninen Scan Agile message approved for testausOSY. Should enroll myself, you had some interesting stuff again.
Fixing testing that is not broken by adding bureacracy feels annoying. Could I just test for a change, allergic to "process improvement".
RT @markotaipale: Get rid of micromanagement: ask "what do you want me to get done" instead "what do you want me to do?" #pm #scrum #agile
I don't work well without preparation in a meeting of "let's write a plan together". I think by writing, and need to restructure the text.
Where does the idea come from that if you set up a project, things get done. There's more projects than people. Missing agile...
How people who favor thinking the need over filling a template work with people who just need the template filled. Multi-customer planning..
I want us to test against the intent written into specification. The text usually does not coney intent too well, esp. detailed spec.
Been thinking about my test data -related presentation. Tried that drawing all on whiteboard, and works. May come too fast with ppt.
Stuck with discussion on what is included in customer acceptance testing. Would rather test not argue over contract-related stuff.
Helped remove another obstacle today - just keep eyes on the goal, not the plan. There's many routes to where ever one's heading...
Bug reporting best practice if you can do it in hundreds of different ways depending on context? Same idea for SBT eurostar webinar intro.
Some marketing work required to get higher-up managers to understand how well things are testing-wise at work. Potential for even better.
Wrote a test specification today. Documented four test cases where I know the expectation was to write out 200. Need change of status quo.
Nice example of incremental automation, but a misunderstanding of brain-engaged testing in intro...
Seems the concept of always testing something different with the tester time is not obvious. Regression test by tester a must?
a question on my 4 tests spec: use relative sizes in metrics since 200 would look better. Could I just test and report the issues...
After a long time, blogged in English on attempts to change the testing world in small scale "Timing is essential": http://bit.ly/fXxKmj
Wondering how much effort one can put on contractor distrust in regression testing. There's a place where mgrs have more clue than testers.
I'm tempted to suggest fake report saying things that they want automated always work if that is the only way to aoid checking them.
Next to refine lean-inspired style of testing with our limited resources. Essential challenge left is finetuning metrics we want to create.
Will pass on the message of CAST 2011 to Finnish Testing Community. Promos like this make it easy: http://youtu.be/gbCgpUhP8oM

@CuriousAgilist @lanettecream @jbtestpilot If you look at someone who writes test automation, they explore like crazy trying to figure out on level of details why their script isn't doing exactly what they want. @CuriousAgilist @lanettecream @jbtestpilot And when the automation runs unattended and fails, what do they do? They find the need to explore why automation failed, because they were surprised. It's like an invitation to explore.

What makes #ExploratoryTesting and #TestAutomation different (if any) is our fixed beliefs in opportunity cost. We fail to recognize that with modern programming, there's much more examples of programming helping you explore than slowing you down.
Also, how fast or slow we are while testing does not define either #ExploratoryTesting or #TestAutomation. The latter focuses on optimizing for when we are away which is a key part of the former too.

Lesson 1. Testing is not using the system. You need to be more driven to information and understanding. More intentional. Many testers need to practice intent.
Lesson 2. Intent is not enough. Serendipity happens through elements of play and making unplanned connections. Awareness of what you know and how you know it becomes essential.
Lesson 3. You are in control. When system gives you a hard constraint, there are still ways you can work through that constraint. If you can simplify or isolate, do that. Complex can happen later.
Lesson 4. Testability. When something is hard to do, remember there’s a developer somewhere who needs to share the pain to build smarter next time.
Lesson 5. You got tools. Find them. You pull in what you need, not rely on just what you’re given.
Lesson 6. Yes, that automation of permutations integrated with vocabulary would come in handy. What you can’t find but want, you can build.
Lesson 7. It really does not calculate scores right. But does that matter - what is quality for this game? What creates emotions relevant enough to impact user’s behavior?
Lesson 8. Randomly hijacking colleagues to playtesting is fun. Should do this more often. I feel energized.

"I don't do twitter fights anymore" from JB indicates he has learned something while not saying what he has actually learned. I am happy with this one.

Conclusion: I cannot say I witnessed a reason for me to keep alienating them from the community. The test automation attacking, even if milder and less going off tangent than back in the days, was still there and I wish it wasn't.
End of reporting. I keep my stance that I refuse to use old stuff as reason of excluding people. I know I may be the only one to forgive, but I have.

If she defends her self when blamed for other people’s mistakes, she gets a manager discussion on her tone. She’s typecasted as someone who is difficult.

The young woman isn’t me. But it’s like I’m looking at the mirror of my past. Having to deal with the regular manager interventions. Having to learn new ways of defending myself. Having to accept that the only way forward it out. Changing myself.

I found someone I will mentor. I’ll teach them about gaslighting, tone policing, mansplaining and expecting we men to do emotional labor of men’s emotions. I’ll help them turn up the positive. Regardless of this shit, women are needed to build great software that runs the world.

I’ve been doing very deliberate #ExploratoryTesting last weeks, aiming for a thing to get started on its continuous releases. This testing I frame under gap analysis: others came before me and tested. What do I still see on top of that?

Out of that testing, I came out with a bunch of bugs we fixed but more importantly, understanding of what it is we’ve built, what threatened its value (way beyond bugs) and a checklist of 35 ‘feature’ test cases, 6 and 6 ‘scenario’ test cases.

My list helps me remember things beyond clicking and seeing it and it works as before. I’ve got test automation on multiple levels for that. They’re boxes to direct thinking, not a list of clicks and past behaviors.

My list is also a model of software in my head that makes my colleagues express how they are surprised I know things they don’t and I’m new. It allows me to show up and help correct the next gaps as they’re emerging, in collaboration with people.

The core of #ExploratoryTesting is in the learning and using that learning everywhere to continue testing. Noticing discrepancies not in the app code only but in how people talk about it - its current state as well as its future.
Good luck automating that. Creating smarter documentation from parts of that, sure. Creating autoclickers and auto references, sure. But if that’s sufficient, we can automate all programming.

The new tools ‘automating exploratory testing’ are to that goal what IDEs are to ‘automating programming’. And that’s helpful. I love an IDE with great refactoring support. It makes coding more joyful. But we rarely say ‘automated refactoring’.
The new tools are automated monkey testing (button clicking) + #ApprovalTesting. They won’t find the features you didn’t implement. But they can be helpful as new ways to replace testing of webUI.

If your current webUI tests are already hooked into a model, the walker through your app can grow beyond monkey testing with #ModelBasedTesting. That also adds the idea of state into your #ApprovalTesting.

Let's talk about model-based testing. Or more like, I talk to make notes of the way I model model-based testing. My history with it is longer than I care to remember as one of my past work places was heavily in that space leading me to research it extensively.

Model-based testing isn't the idea that "all testing is based on models" just like risk-based testing isn't the idea that "all testing is based on risk. All testing is based on models and risk, but still these techniques are more specific.

Model-based testing is the idea that we could create a concrete model that would capture relevant information in a way that is transferrable to new people (captures things better than words alone) and follows a set of rules that enables us to describe it in programmable format.

It feels like the testing equivalent of what UML was trying to do, expect it isn't just UML. UML as I recall it, was trying to create 4+1 perspectives to capture it all. Model-based testing takes any model if it is useful for testing purposes.

Usually the model I see is state model. And we can model so many things as state. User interface transitions. Functionality. Anything where one thing leads to another. And when we have state models, we can try using those to generate paths through the model.

These models, for testing purposes give us two things. They give us a concise way of describing things leading to things, and a way of saying partially that this should lead here with an oracle. It enables generating test cases that have a type of asserts attached to them.

I know my friend @ru_altom works in the space of all good things testing, including model-based testing. She shared an example of using python, altwalker and a set of selenium  page objects to move from creating scripts to creating models with my old team.

The demo Ru did was on the last week before I quit the company. I hoped it would catch on but I had little power as I was leaving. I hear they tried it at a new feature. What I learned discussing their experience is what fascinates me today.

It feels like we all are looking for that one way to do all things testing. We should stop that. There is a mix of ways, this enables you to do stuff you did not do before but you still will miss the old style of linear, easy to read tests too.

When things fail with a model, there is an abstraction there that makes pinpointing the problem one step harder. It's a tradeoff on getting that versatility to your scripts. Granularity - saying exactly what is wrong - is inherent in unit tests, but not model-based tests.

When you build that model, it is easy to do too complex. It is a specific technique that requires skills of that technique. But there is no better way to learn that try and FAIL - it is only your First Attempt in Learning.

Also, you may end up questioning who should build that model. What if machine learning was up for building that model, instead of you doing the work. It gives your automation efforts an extra shape you can start pondering on.

For many many years, Finland had multiple research projects in the space of model-based testing. I got to hear and read what they did. And to note that good stuff from university research does not stick easily with companies.

They found *critical* problems in the research partner's applications. They were quietly fixed. They publicized finding problems with relatively small effort in publicly available new sites. Crashing type of problems, easiest of the oracles.

When I first joined, I was totally confused on how little people told me. It felt like I had to get to everything the hard way. For a moment I confused the lack of help to being mean or testing to see if people fail. It was neither.

The key people in the team believed that you'll ask what you need. Prematurely teaching you things when you are not pulling it isn't a great way of taking things forward. Always being there to answer questions, and help when pulled is a great way of taking things forward.
It turned out that people and helping your team mates was really a priority. You'd express confusion, and their priority was to help you get through it. Best team ever.
We scheduled our work as it was pulled. We pulled work from others. We understood that everything is pulled from the perspective of having something different in production.

The disciplines that have made me the type of tester I am today, with the impact I can make, today. Building on a foundation of curiosity, persistence and being ok of not being ready while being useful. Spoiler: programming isn't one of them.

Folks, including myself, keep saying testers need to learn programming. But I say that almost like "every child in the world needs to learn programming". We need to learn programming to understand that computers, for now, abide to our choices not the other way around.

Unfortunately as per my experiences, programming discipline for tester is important to get harassers off your back. So next time you tell testers they need to code, evaluate your reasons of saying so. Grant them power, don't remove power they already have as humans.

The three important disciplines to grow, for me, have been 1) software architecture (and as per conway's law, designing teams to create architectures). 2) economics 3) social sciences as in how to work with people in various socioeconomic structures.

On 2) economics, you both need to know where money to your salary comes from, but also know how to recognize value, cost and opportunity cost. Tell good, founded stories around those and it grows your impact.

I've been thinking about online conferences and recordings, a theme that @lisacrispin got me thinking of. It is fascinating to notice how quickly we shifted, even with webinars, into more 'production value' prerecording (and editing) out talks.

I believe the better experience for our audiences online for talks comes from the speakers and conferences focusing on the production value. Recording, retaking, editing, overlays of slides and faces, moving focus - all these add to the value of watching something online.

We need interactive sessions too, but they are a different design all together. If we want, we can do a mix of shorter prerecorded and an online activity. The amount of work for delivering with this idea has shifted significantly.

Previously as a speaker, you could show up, talk, have a conversation and be done with it. Whatever process you had coming to a point where you had a talk you could deliver varied significantly. The ones that are rehearsed to fluency tend to be better.

Now the production value creation can be split between the speaker and the conference in a lot of ways. I just delivered a talk where I needed to record me standing up (felt overwhelmed) and send slides separately. I have no clue how they edit all of that together, it's 4 months!

A few weeks ago I delivered a 30 minute talk that took me 5 hours to record. I messed up recording first round leaving out voice track. Second round I got interrupted on. Third round I messed up scheduling my message. Editing tool ate some version.

Yet, I would rather do this than show up for the conference organizers only to deliver that session so that they record it. It's like real session but no audience. If there is editing value, it might be captions. Yet captions are promiseware.

So, what I ended up with is that instead of me thinking of it as recording the talk, this new style gives me chances on really properly doing some editing I would like to see. Which leads me to my final problem for now.

Can I reuse a talk ever after this or did my talks now turn into one delivery only? There are people who were already tired of regular speakers telling same old same old, but when it is THE EXACT SAME, it is no longer even paying for the performance, just access to the video.

I paired with @swalchemist yesterday, and now that I have properly rested after it, I want to make my notes of the experience available to him and the rest of you. First off: lovely experience. He did a great job selecting us something to work on when all we had was an hour.

The work he selected was a bug fix, an expected but missing behavior. He introduced the idea of having old vs. new implementations he was porting, with new having a bug the old didn't. The first appearance of it all is a wall of code.

Having unit tests around was great. It was great we could do our change adding a test that fails even if zoom remote control refused to let me type the necessary characters. With running all tests for first commit, the existing tests found a bug we had introduced.
Working with him again reminded me how unit tests keep us grounded. How those fails turn to passes and forgotten, and often not even visible to testers.

While we were pairing, he talked of a few concepts through the code we browsed. Lombok and avoiding having to write getters and setters yourself. Patterns, and the variety of options where were. Design choices in the moment.

What I appreciate the most at first though was to notice how he automated within automated tests. The modeling of a concept where the details shouldn't matter, and abstracting that away into something that was automatic. We should teach that in testing.

I learned something about myself again, as with every pair I ever work with. When faced with unknown and a wall of code, I choose something that I do. In this case, I could track the work. This ended up as forgetting in the end, and remembering right after.
Also, I learned that I envy people who get to do pairing continuously. Thanks for the fun experience, @swalchemist.

@lucianadrian It is such a simple thing though: you look at you stakeholder groups and find the right way to work with them. Even if agile focuses on the team, the team practices are only one set of practices to figure out.

I learned the concept of "flight levels" at @BrewingAgile this  year, and it immediately clicked as a way of explaining what we had been doing with my particularly good and successful team. There were three "practice layers" we were working on: team, cross-team, management.

On team level, we had a lot of those "no" practices. No jira, no estimates, no scrum master, no product owner, no projects. We recreated our backlog every three months, and threw it away after. We recreated our work list every two weeks and threw it away after.

On cross-team level, we fostered a networked communication model. No one was responsible for representing the team towards others. Everyone was. Everyone fished, and brought home the fish they acquired. New folks were given a piece of network they'd prioritize.

On business management side the model would have needed the most work. We listened carefully, on many forums. But it always felt one-sided. If we had known this layer was incomplete, we might have fixed it. Instead, we let it be.

On team level, the practice of maintaining a good balance of discovery and delivery work, with bias to action was valuable. Separating discovery to other people was generally a bad idea because of handoff. Discovery centered around the dev implementing was good.

We also had zero bug policy, a stop-the-line policy and developer-centric ways of working to emphasize documenting as code that then runs in production. Whether that production is customer's or our own system to keep work ongoing.

Things that can only happen when isolating... 
I was about to leave for downtown to record a talk for #MimmitKoodaa. As I stepped out the door, I realized we have snow. I had no winter tires. Wait, it gets better (1/n).
I called a sister with winter tires to give me a ride. She agreed and left home but forgot her bag home. The bag had car keys AND home keys. She was locked out. Wait, it still continues. (2/n)

She called another sister to open the door. That one was on other side of city but agreed to come right away. Then it turns out she needed also to be somewhere to pick up one of the kids. One more stop on the route, and we were on. But wait, it still continues (3/n)

We got downtown, parked and walked to the recording location. I was supposed to do a demo talk, and would need to use my computer. It wasn't good for camera, so the first sister turned into my strong-style pairing partner, hands off camera. True to using words to test. (4/n)

With the session setup being hectic, the first step of my testing found a problem in my environment. A web application without internet connection does not lend itself to testing. Navigating with "fix it" was sufficient. The pair was awesome! (5/n)

We continued with the testing, the camera blocking the part of screen where all error messages were. Not a recommended thing to try navigating with half a screen. But true to exploratory testing, we shifted testing and got stuff done. (6/n)

Then the little things you do without realizing got in the way. I brushed back my hair with my hand, and the microphone broke. We still continued testing, I held the mic with my hand. They came about to fix it while we tested. (7/n)

With all things going off track, I realized how lucky I was in the first place. I had a sister that could drive as my pair with me because of the snow. And this is how we work on complex things. Pairing. Learning. Adjusting. And continuing. This is ExploratoryTesting. (8/8)

Some common adjectives and their meaning on a tester. ‘Agile’: does not do testing but process and coaching. Preaches whole-team. ‘Modern’: Tools and automation, and telemetry - testing in production. ‘Automation’: writes lots of code with occasional idea of it being valuable.

‘Manual’: spends time experiencing the application like users and stakeholders, even on an API level. Focuses on observation. ‘Exploratory’: takes manual further to new info, using code extend to activities humans don’t reach.
We need all five not one of the above. It is super rare to get it all in one package in a way where they can also deliver on five roles.

Thinking of the words to describe there's two kinds of testing. Testing of code we create, and testing of systems the code ends up in. I really don't like the word "unit testing", as it gets us into a discussion of unit.

When we test the code we create, we usually get four benefits from that testing: spec, feedback, regression, granularity. Those are essentially different when we do TDD vs. test-after. Loving TDD. But test-after is better than skipping testing of code and way too many do that.

Testing of systems the code ends up in is split to creating systems that test systems, and testing systems. It's like understanding the domain to being able to automate it. Too many people in the testing the code world miss relevant aspects around testing the systems.

It's not either or. It is both. And the modern optimization problem around testing is that you no longer can optimize one (testing of systems) like testers used to. Testing of code enables new ways to look at the whole.
@BischoffDev I hate all three. So I try this: testing of code we create vs. testing of systems the code ends up in. I also would like to talk about size of feedback cycles. :)
@testinsideout @Maaikees No, that’s another dimensions.

@wolframkriesing End-to-End tests may cover a lot of ground and be fine as long as they are mostly passing. But when they fail, granularity is bad and delaying feedback inevitable. I find we are always struggling with the balance, and having more of unit tests is a winning approach.

Thinking back my history of #AgileTesting and #Agile in general. I started with it while we called it lightweight methods, as a researcher of those methods. That was year 2000.

My first ever public talk is on testing in Extreme Programming, in 2001. While I had already experiences in stepping towards Agile Testing, none of the teams I worked with had done XP - the talk put together my experiences and stuff I read on books and articles.

In 2003, I published an article trying to make sense in how the chance in cadence that agile brought along impacted testing as I knew it. The article was called "Increasing Understanding of the Modern Testing Perspective in Software Development Projects".
In 2005, I started a job in an organization that was just moving to Agile in scale. It was not a single team doing XP type of thing, but tens of teams doing a system for large numbers of users.

Even if I relied on what "agile" was in the books and by manifesto by then, it is now over 15 years of me living agile testing. I took a job in that timeframe to deepen my understanding of how it was different in non-agile projects, and this agile stuff changes everything.

When we do, we figure out same things independently, but also through being inspired by other people's efforts. Figuring out how to move testing to continuous releases became my signature move. In scale where we previously needed "system testing teams", I dismantled many.

During 15 years, I stopped caring about #Agile and #AgileTesting. I did not recognize either as my home ground. Agile became scrum. Agile testing became "whole team testing". My home ground is #ModernAgile and #ContinuousDelivery.

For me, agile testing involves being able to test large things and yet release continuously. It's cadence, feedback loops and feeling at ease because risk does not accrue. It's the idea that one class of people don't "stay to test for release this weekend" but we enjoy normalcy.

Organizations still need this transformation to testing (and development) normalcy. They may say they are Agile already, and not have that. And getting there is not implementing a method, but understanding how to get to pull and flow, systems and value thinking.

I may broadcast the idea that I have been around doing this for a while. Yet most of my days go into just doing it. The people who do this and have practical experience are often hidden, silent - focused on doing it.

We have a simulator that runs in automated and manual mode generating data to a pattern or something you chose. That means we have now test automation that has automated-manual combo running unattended.

Since last night, I have been thinking of the baggage that keynotes come for me. And by baggage, I mean mental load. You might imagine the mental load is about getting to address a major audience. That would be great. That would be normal. But mine is different.

In aspiring to become a keynoter, I had worked on being a speaker for 10 years. A popular speaker, then program committee chairman for EuroSTAR posted about "no women of merit". 10 years speaking wasn't a merit. I wasn't native English speaker and thus more invisible.

4,5 years ago I finally got to do my 1st keynote, after 15 years of speaking. The keynote itself was great. But the other keynoter, a prominent tester using half of his talk to talk about me on things that aren't about me sucked. https://t.co/hR02ejM1Rp

Being told from stage by another keynoter that I'm not authentic and compassionate, that I don't think discussion is important, and that I believe on not focusing attention and energy is an interesting interpretation.

Just to note: I still think debate is something that needs to be consensual. Forcing debate on people isn't ok. Debate is also competitive, and in most cases I believe we want to build something together not shoot the other one down. But I debate too.

I posted that picture on twitter, and the guy lost some jobs. But I now have the baggage of remembering that there are people like that, and conference organizers who don't invite me back after I defend myself.

I don't only defend myself. I was just reminded yesterday that 3,5 years ago, I did my first really big international keynote. And in the sidelines of that keynote, another prominent guy in testing lost some jobs.
In going to that conference, I had just discovered that the person who had invited me to keynote had made very inappropriate propositions to new women testers aspiring to become speakers.

By the time I took the stage in front of over 1000 people, the guy was no longer running that conference. He had introduced three other keynotes in that conference, and was no longer there to introduce me.
I had used some of my energy, and taken a major personal risk in seeking consequences for his actions. I got lucky. But it is now a part of my keynoting experience.

From "no women of merit", to keynotes on topic but on the sidelines having to deal with social justice, a keynote is never that straightforward for me. 
Thankfully only 2 have been that draining. 
But I wonder: how many other people have been this "lucky".

The women coming after me deserve - by my experience and their own brilliance - have it easier. Safety comes with work, and caring for this stuff. My hardships are part of me but I wish they would not be part of what comes for people after me.

If your talk is not about your experience but a general idea, and your understanding of the idea is limited, you may refer to experts in the audience.
If your talk is about about your experience, and question is about your experience, you may still refer to experts in the audience to use their status to add credibility to what you shared.
If your talk is about your experience but the question seeks to generalize, you may refer to experts in the audience to generalize. But you may serve your audience better with responding yourself.

In most cases through, the speaking slot is reserved for you. If there is a question, it is for you. Choosing to make space for a wider conversation as your Q&A is a possibility, but it means also denying access to you on your Q&A. You may want that.
In many cases even if not all, your audience came to hear you and they have other chances to go hear that other expert. Don't take away your audience's chance of learning from your experience.
If the talk isn't experience-based, you might want to frame it as that. It starts with setting expectations.

@jlottosen A common advice on Q&A for new speakers is that they can ask the audience if they get a question they can't deal with in the moment. They could also choose to say "I don't know" and focus on the questions they do know, especially if there is a queue of questions.

Let's talk about system testing, with example of Robot Framework. The core group there released a version 4 recently, and the quality experience they created in the few places I have now looked at is fascinating.

Thinking in terms of systems, there is quite an ecosystem of libraries, plugins, whatever around that core. When they made 4 available, it seems they weren't waiting or coordinating the ecosystem of parts around it together.

The experience where I was looking at it is a day where jenkins jobs went crazy reporting things that were not true. There were two reasons for that. 1) they changed priorities of tests, a central concept 2) they didn't update jenkins plugin before availability.

Obviously, we would not see the trouble if we did not allow for changes to be pulled automatically. I could talk in length about the pros and cons of each approach, and I am happy with pulling new even with risk of breaking.

The experience could have been very different. There could be a way of users knowing why things are changing. There could have been availability of matching jenkins plugin. Instead, after release they started thinking about matching changes.

Where I work isn't the only place that lost a day to not attending to the ecosystem. I may be the only one who wrote that down on the costs of being a part of this ecosystem. Adding it to the list of misses I keep tabs on.

The list started with one major miss: suggesting that testers won't be paid while developers do on a robot framework foundation project. In a community of testers, the foundation of paying for the work of testers missing is a big red flag in my books.

Free tools aren't free. This tool costs plenty, both in direct costs, and opportunity costs. It costs people careers, even if it gives it to some. It costs in supporting injustice. And for the last year, it has lived rent-free in my brain because I am giving it a change.

Exploratory testing is not a step in a pipeline. It is an approach driving design of pipelines. It is the reaction to a pipeline when not green. The manual step to hang out on UI with an open mind is not it.

Most of my exploratory testing takes place before the pipeline starts on commit AND after it completely finishes, in production. Production is great for exploratory testing beyond basic hygiene of features.
Pipelines don't do programming and testing. They run automation. It's a road we built to production.

Doing a talk on #BDD internally walked me through to a realization. I have done #discovery, #formulation and #automation all separately but never as connected three practices. I found value in each separately for a purpose.

My experiences of #discovery are example mapping workshops, and how talking in examples truly helps us get on the same page. Yet, in those projects we never cared to keep the examples. The transformation to code was implicit, through understanding in team.

My experiences of #formulation are around thinking I understood and modeled requirements better to show what we were missing. The structure helped me "shift left" and get business and programmer in sync. But I thought I already "got it" on the domain.

The experiences around #automation are plenty. There is, however, rarely the need of business readable format where I have been. Translating previous agreements from code-like format when needed has been a lot less tedious than maintaining executable requirements.

Looking at the work we do for "testing", it is no longer a one role job. 1) We build hardware prototypes. From artificial skies to resistor replacements to something fancier, to building shelfs of cards on racks with remote control with a lot of versatility.

2) We build test systems - code to run code and hardware, and help us figure out changes and their impacts. It's more than regression test automation, and has more dimensions in building because of the hardware. I still think automating powering something off is interesting.

3) We integrate in scales that are unusual to me. Prototypes of various sorts, ready systems of various sorts, with a variety of protocols, payloads and purposes. Some of our integrations are brittle to factors I have not analyzed before and enjoy getting at now.

4) We figure out specs and their limitations for versatile use cases. The most traditional "testing" that I would think of. Would this work, what does it mean that it works, and what of this people care of.

It is an honor to keynote at #esconfs like I will this year, but is also, for me, a result of hard work. EuroSTAR is the conference that made me resolute on becoming a keynote speaker in the first place.

April, 2015 was when my spite-driven development started and twitter was the platform. The conference had published their lineup with usual lack of representation of genders and the movement of publicly mentioning it was just starting.

A group of testers in the community loosely connected with the conference started making a point of "no women of merit". 2015 I had been doing public speaking for 14 years and took offense in the lack of merit. Because it's now merit I was missing. It was opportunity.

I did not know it then, but I know it now: merit in keynoting is experience in keynoting. Getting experience requires experience. You need to get lucky to get started. I started looking for that luck.

I got lucky to know @QA_nna who invited me to keynote in her conference in New York. It took me years to realize that I had already keynoted before, in MoT single track conferences. That realization I got from @SelenaDelesie that called her talk keynote.

In practice all talks in single track conference could be keynotes. The invited ones where you did not need to submit a proposal to be selected are definitely that even when there is only one track. You choose what you call it.

My first big international keynote was with the STAR-conferences in US. I loved the stage that @awadesqe held for me, and the positive of that experience outweigh all things going on under the surface both in community and personally.

The keynote that I have enjoyed the most is with DDD Europe. Getting to know that community and meeting @mathiasverraes as organizer was great. It felt like closure to work on bridging a gap of communities for me in personal level.

Hard work includes becoming the person that has the experiences that resonate work the stage, but also saying yes to opportunities, traveling and being away. And everyone and everything in the journey was not supportive.

The first keynote I delivered was the keynote where the other keynoter decided to use their keynote to talk about *me* instead of their topic and it changed testing community significantly. People united against bullying.

For the big international keynote, I had to deal with an inner circle man telling me they handed me that keynote that was theirs, and go confirming that this was not the case. It was never theirs but the betrayal I felt with the claim was hard to deal with.

Best part of this is the people. I've made friends, around the world, people I would not have met otherwise. Some of the connections remain. Some people collect locations, I collect people. And I appreciate my collection of great people.

Brief history of #ExploratoryTesting. Introduced by Cem Kaner in '80s to describe smart way real companies were doing testing that was different as it avoided separating test design and test execution, maintaining tester agency and learning.

Before the term, companies were doing it. I have found descriptions of doing it in Finnish references from the 60s and 70s. Coining the term was recognizing practitioners were doing something special.

Anything and everything the communities at large have published on exploratory testing are descriptions of things people in the companies are inventing. It's not academic research creating this. It is software people observing and describing real-world patterns.

A lot of co-describing was done in peer conferences lead by Prof. Kaner. He brought together practitioners, consultants and academics. Consultants and academics did publishing the lessons into reusable models. It is all community-inspired.

#ExploratoryTesting is created in multiple places at the same time and while copyright applies to a published piece, it isn't the same thing as trademark that requires more novelty to acquire. Attribution is not legal requirement, it is practice of recognizing *previous work*.

Attribution means crediting the source where information or a direct quotation was obtained if it wasn't your own firsthand knowledge. We have a lot of own firsthand knowledge that exists having tested 5 - 10 - 25 years.

Attribution is done to seek credibility through multiple sources in academic writing, it is - again - not a legal requirement. Stuff we do is less valuable than stuff a million people do same way we do. And value is not money. It's knowledge.

Academic care for attribution also has a purpose of showing novelty - their own advancement. Attribution as practice is intended to allow your own contribution to stand out and shine. #Testing field uses weaponized attribution a lot.

The session on #ExploratoryTesting at #EuroSTARconf really highlighted why I separate #ExploratoryTesting and #Testing and refuse the 3.0 "all testing is exploratory" advice: (test) managers and developers still think giving someone a list of "run these daily" is testing.

Both Adam and Dorota had started their careers under bad management. I had not. I had bad managers later. Before I was introduced to idea that made my testing worse, I had already a foundation of better. That is #ExploratoryTesting.

If the core of #ExploratoryTesting is bad management, boy do I have some stories to tell. Like hiring a junior who knew someone in the company, and took their advice on writing test cases more seriously than my advice on focusing on results that matter.

Or another junior who followed my teaching and did great, but got advice from the other senior they knew to only focus on negative tests. "Try too big values", "Try disconnecting it while it is doing things", ending up with lots of low value bugs and lost reputation.

Or the manager who insisted I would not work if I did not show my test cases because testing is the crappiest job he can imagine. He did the best he can to make it such by insisting on the wrong thing....

History loops back. On the #EuroSTARconf Q&A for my keynote 'Test Automationist's Gambit', someone asks about Conformiq model based test automation tool. I was responsible for testing it long long time ago, and it is a great story I should tell sometime.

Back in those days, I was a senior consultant and the company made so much money on selling me to other companies that they let me manage the testing but not do the testing. My time with testing of the testing tool was significantly limited.

Instead, we hired cheaper consultants to do the testing. They had been on my testing course, and their comment changed how I talk about testing. As I introduced how they'd test: "It is great that we are doing this the smart way and not like you taught at university."

I had not paid attention to the discrepancy of how I taught test case design (expected) and exploratory testing. I have not been able to avoid paying attention since. We laughed together the test cases from earlier testing - page after page of steps in test tool, saying nothing.
Automation != Regression. That is not appreciating at all what work we do in testing with automation.

We test unique paths as we build the automation. New values to same flows are parameters. Automation takes us where we want to start attended testing from. It covers environments and combos otherwise beyond our reach. It alerts on change that isn’t regression and we learn.

The first is requirements - tests traceability. I’m firmly in the ‘minimize’ camp. Or even ‘avoid’. I understand it. I think it has made a lot of testing worse.

The second is learned organizational role-based helplessness. Also known as silo mentality. Testers not fixing bugs. Testers not deciding on releases.    Developers not scheduling meetings but expecting managers to do it.

The third is definitely now end of fully remote work. The idea of returning to office isn’t exciting. The hybrid work model makes remote a bad experience. Full remote was the great equalizer for remote team members.
As fourth I must mention ‘process’. The idea that we scale good by giving general guidelines that must be fulfilled. The recipes of mediocrity.

Fifth and final for today is learning time outside working time. Seriously, we don’t want people who aren’t honing their skills. It’s work. Tools need sharpening. Brains are tools. 1.01^365 = 37.8. One percent every day. Win over past self.

People keep asking how to get management let you do exploratory testing. But the other things they say mean often they don't know what they are asking for.

It's not about asking for time hanging out doing something no one can explain. It's about structuring your whole testing to enable learning and results. It's not a "throw extra time in". It is using all your time in smart ways.

It is not about "no documentation", but about necessary documentation as output. It is not about "no test cases" but about choosing focuses that provide you a sandbox and a motivation. It's not separate of automation!!!

The only reason organizations need to separate automation and exploratory testing is that they haven't been cultivating both skills in same people or the skill of collaboration that enables people to truly share work using different skills on single task simultaneously.

Even if zoom-beep problem made pairing in a demo session today harder than it should be, I thoroughly enjoyed it. I also scheduled another round of rehearsing with the pair that volunteered today with automateIT session on contemporary #ExploratoryTesting.

The process of how you create accurate test cases? That's #ExploratoryTesting. The difference comes on times when you repeat - do you walk the same paths (scripted) or allow yourself to maximize your results (exploratory).

How do we learn a new automation tool? By exploring and trying to apply it in work it is intended for. That is #ExploratoryTesting. Too much learning on the same time is impossible, so we layer things to the speed the person doing the testing can cope with.

It is difficult to explain the difference in how I look at an application when I do #ExploratoryTesting and how someone with less experience looks at it. I would be up for trying to have two isolated experiences with some test target described and compared.

As I listen to Ed Manlike on #SauceCon on Robot Framework, I am thinking again on why I am still against - he does a great job presenting the positives on this talk, better than most people. It's the practice that I see that makes me aversive.
While it is a natural language programming language, it is separate from whatever other language already resident in the team. This drives it to become a language of specialist testers.

For its users in the wild except for few exceptional users, it creates a box that confines them, rather than levels them up. The ecosystem size and style of communication leave people in companies struggling.

The idea of it being special skill (as its own language) causes people in teams in assuming they have nothing to contribute to the "specialists". It works, in practice that I observe, against whole-team testing. It creates magic experts who aren't really experts.

It comes with a lot of inefficiencies. Like the debugging stuff, that you can find if someone tells you how. You need to find robocorp and know that is the same thing and tune a little to get the stuff to use. So for long time I said it does not exist - that hard to discover.

And my recent pet peeve. It makes my colleagues claim that only robot framework could be used for testing embedded systems. After you have programmatic APIs to hardware and software, anything that sits on top works for you.

Continuous testing is this idea that it is important to keep running same tests continuously with automation so that we always know if earlier results for those tests are still valid.
Agile testing is this idea that whole team should be collaborating and testing in short iterations of product creation.
Holistic testing is this idea that testing isn't only happening with delivery but also on discovery, and we have a lot of different activities under the testing umbrella.
Maintaining automation is human-centric testing. We have not automated maintaining and creating automation. We're trying in space of AI but not there yet.
"Let's do some exploratory testing there" speaks in technique perspective of exploratory testing. I try to frame it in my head as "Let's do some *more* exploratory testing there".
I might like holistic testing if they didn't keep promoting exploratory testing as a technique, always with the pyramid with the cloud on top. The cloud looms over the entire pyramid, folks.
