Do I or should I care about cross-browser testing? Depends on what we build on browser. In a lot of cases, my answer is no. I don't and shouldn't, because the issues we need to find we find by choosing one. But I have some exceptions, usually based on frameworks built upon.

@AutomatedTester If my team is building a webUI that works on the browser, the browser bugs are relevant to my team when they make our application misbehave. And the choices my team makes on how simple things we run on browser will have a significant impact. That is all I say.

@AutomatedTester On knowing you would rely on 1) users complaining 2) team using their own app on different browsers 3) sometimes dedicating time on just seeing things you don't see by accident. This is how I come to conclusion that I don't want to always run cross-browser TA.

While I acceptance test what we rely on, I test what we build very differently than the things we use. Except when results show that I need to test what we rely on.

@AutomatedTester I started off my career testing localisations, and every OS language tier was essentially different. I believed all language versions of OS must be tested on until I realized the architecture of how language is provided is different. Sometimes 1 OS / 1 OS language is good enough.

@AutomatedTester There is always two parts to how I would consider these: the suggestions to keep my projects/company successful, and the suggestions to invest in a better world worth living. A lot of the proposals I make are on the first, always battling with time to invest.

@AutomatedTester I did not say test on one browser. I said *automate on one browser* unless your application implementation gives you reasons to automate on many, and test on all but not continuously.

My 'cross-browser' approach depends on the tech we build on. We build on our own react components. If I had to build on odoo, drupal or wordpress, I might believe differently. The more complex the tech is you are running your thing on, the more you need to test across browsers.

Today I am discovering the core lessons from my talk by listening to myself speak. 

1. Prefer empty paper with a frame. It encourages integrating diverse perspectives in ways reviewing someone else's result never will. 

2. Testing is applied steganography. Bugs are invisible ink of conversations we should be having. 

3. Everything that does not need to be automated gets done while automating. This is subject to how you organize for testing. Do more of it on unit testing level.

I went to look for more info from the main source of definition and oh boy, there is a foundational problem. Machine learning (the technology - as interviewees discussed it) and machine learning (the capability - as book defines it) are two entirely different things.

The capabilities *intended* for this research are: 
1) natural language processing to communicate successfully in a human language
2) knowledge representation to store what it knows or hears
3) automated reasoning to answer questions and to draw new conclusions
4) machine learning to adapt to new circumstances and to detect and extrapolate patterns. 
5) computer vision and speech recognition to perceive the world
6) robotics to manipulate objects and move about.
ML the technology is part of 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. 6 could be possibly *just* automation but most likely also ML the technology is part of it too.

"How do you test localisations", I asked. Received a test case. Mentioned I knew that, but I did not know why they go through the moves they do. Turns out neither did they. 

Drilled down into risks:
- some (new) strings may not be localizable
- the original and the localised file may have differences in contents and a missing string may cause problems
- there may be missing translated texts
- the translated texts may be mistranslated 
... 

If you rely on "test case", document why not just how.

A week ago I hijacked a teams test planning and did a plan that follows change. I reviewed the very small number of commits changing things from last accepted baseline, and created a table of my observations. I listed names of components changing, functional areas those components are part of and if with the change came unit tests. 

My theory that I worked with in analysis is that changes in unit tests represent 1) tests failing and compulsory fixing or 2) dev thinking about testing the change.

Especially if 2) is true, it lowers a particular type of risk. 

Similarly, I know all of the devs and know which ones would never send out a change without trying it themselves, and which ones shortcut. So "who" changes things is part of the analysis.

The output document I created confused the next planner who got lost on a week of detailed unit test analysis. 

Lesson learned: look at effort to produce an output. The process you imagine may be different from the one applied.

Three types of training: 
1. Summaries. "Here's what the world seems to think about X"
2. War stories. "Here's me living through X"
3. Experiential. "Here's a simulation of X for your to try"

1 and 2 can be done with articles and books if people read, or with podcast and videos if they listen and watch. 3 requires classroom and every group is different.

I used to do a lot of 1&2 as training. Now I do a lot of 3.

I wrote down for a story: 

- What we have without the story
- What we have after the story
- What would be acceptance criteria (rough test plan for quick rejection)
- The story "As a <blah> I want <blah> so that <blah>" 
- Gherkin examples clarifying the story

This is a lot, and still people ask what exactly they will need to code, all the way to error messages.

I tested, and did not like the error message. Following the rule of understanding basic implications I knew there is no localisation impact. So I changed it to better while it may still not be perfect. 

Test failed as it checked for the message on UI (duh), and I fixed the test.

This is what I expect testers to do. Perfect is the enemy of better. Fixing takes less time that reporting and prioritising and so on.

Last week at conference, we ended up analyzing a software interoperability bug that 1) made police enter the apartment 2) made sofa smell of vanilla and 3) sent apartment owner invoice on door opening service they never requested. 

The long story is funny and the conference insight pointed it to a Spotify bug. 

Thread…

The apartment owner left home to a company party. Coming home late at night, nothing special to note. The next morning though - first note of sofa smelling vanilla, as mysteriously a scented oil lamp had fallen down and been broken soaking the sofa. How was unclear, it wasn’t a party result. 

Next was a note on kitchen table, signed by a police unit.

The note tells the police unit had entered the apartment in owners absence, to disconnect speakers. 

More understanding followed when a neighbor worried had been reaching out. There was a real concern of something unusual when speakers had flashed full volume music close to midnight. 

For a year, we joked about Alexa organizing an empty house party that police needed to break ups

With the conference conversation we broke the interoperability into its components. 

First there was Alexa and Sonos, assistant with speaker and a speaker. Both have separate sound controls. Somehow normally turning Alexa sound down had generic impact, but Sonia could still have volume set to full. 

In comes Spotify. It turns out that having connected it to this home system, allowed turning on music while binding it elsewhere. Now with full volume.

So around midnight the phone that usually controlled Spotify at home was at the company party, providing music for the masses. And home. With max volume. 😂😂😂

Neighbors care. Police turns off speakers. And the invoice for this use of mater key nullified after a bit of arguing who pays if Alexa invites police over in need of the later key. 

Best bug ever.

And I’ve been corrected: no music for the party. The music was just for home with the earlier pairing. Since playing music did not make a sound, the phone went back to pocket while sounds were going at other side of the city. 

Alexa empty house party. 😂😂😂

Ru Cindrea is explaining the model-based testing we're doing for our products. We don't want to write scripts for the arrows. And we don't want to write scripts for the invisible arrows. This is why we write interfaces for operations, and model the system.
The UI turns to this - a model you can cover with tools. We do this in python, selenium, altwalker, and graphwalker.
Selenium gives us *real browsers* not just approximation of browsers, and one of the interfaces we drive programmatically. We don't write tests, we write something akin to POM without tests.
Demoable content of coverage while running in green, watching a video is more expressive of what we're doing that me sharing pictures.

#ExploratoryTesting was coined by Cem Kaner in 1988. Well, that is the earliest publication you can find of it, and the storyline says he was using the word earlier to describe the style of skilled multidisciplinary testing common in Silicon Valley. I have found references to this style of testing in 1973 at Kela, the Social Insurance Institution in Finland and attribute some of my learning and enthusiasm on it for long-retired Mervi Hyvönen from Kela.

In its 36+ years of existence, we have learned that people think about it differently. I still to this day struggle explaining the the brand I am teaching is founded on extensive use of automation, but not just regression automation - there is so much more to programmatic testing. So I called my learning brand #ContemporaryExploratoryTesting
We really still don't agree on what it contains. Does it matter? Maybe not except when people are trying to make sense of what experiences they are picking up from what others share.

Trying out calculating code contributor dependency ratio. I calculate it as the time invested by those who contribute average or above to code to those who contribute below average to code.

Four data points to "make a plan". 
1) don't make a plan, just hack. 
2) make a plan, tie to past experiences and focus on where experience is lacking on query

I was updating my web page, when I learned there is a bug in #ConfEngine where a functionality does on work on firefox. Rathole! 

I go to ConfEngine, with the idea of some exploratory testing to learn if this bug can be found with #Selenium and #Playwright tests. We do know that selenium automates browsers while playwright automates approximations of browsers, be it a superset of selected latest branded they have expanded to. Rathole!

Instead of reproducing the bug, I open a repo I have with random scripts in the two, and since its been more than 6 months since I've done this, I find myself doing pip install --upgrade -series. Rathole!

It must be a great idea to write a post about this, since I commented some of this in someone else's post a few days back. I write the post and resume ConfEngine exploration. 

Armed with tools, I realize I did not reproduce the bug. So I do that. And of course it does not reproduce.

But I have a video that shows it reproduces. So I analyze some more of that. I look at the exact browser version, and upgrade mine also to latest, no help. I look at the exact scenario, no help. I look at the addons, and I don't even know what all those are.

Following some of my ideas, I learn I find a way of reproducing a problem that looks like the one, and it is related to user rights. I have some the others don't. Could that be hiding the problem?

However, if that is the problem, then it's not browsers. I know the first reporter would be unlikely to not test on other browsers, and lo behold, the error messages just don't match on the dev tools. Same symptom, different causes. Rathole! 

I write a talk proposal about browser testing and time. Resuming again. 

The error message around cross origin request suggest it has to be settings difference or addon difference, and while it is browser, it's your browser not my browser.

I get interrupted, and speak an hour with a really smart person about Conways law and why things I call architecture can just as well be organization design and we should collaborate to fix both. 

And I still don't know how to set up a browser that would allow me to test if the bug can be found with both #Selenium and #Playwright.  But I suspect that since it's really about the real browser, it can't. 

Long story short, I am on vacation and I can fall into any ratholes I want to and I love it.

On conversation with Dr. Derek Cabrera on UpThinking, we're talking about practicing 5 moves of better thinking. 
- zoom in 
- zoom out
- take other's perspective
- recognize your bias
- see relationships

He is making a point that out of 10 people given a problem, 5 freeze. The 5 that don't freeze, apply moves. 25% do zoom in, 0% zoom out (enterprise thinking). 10% see relationships, <10 % takes other's perspective and 0% recognize their own bias.

#InternationalSystemsThinkingConf
Apparently there are more specific practice things that they call "moves". Kind of like a technique to learn these kinds of things we miss out on when we are trying to solve problems.

Listened to Dr. Gianni DiMarco: Cognitive Biases research report. They looked at describing your thinking and classifying your thinking into Distinctions (identity / other), Systems (part / whole), Relations (action, reaction), and Perspectives (view, point). They discovered this is the order of commonality of people sourcing ideas from, and that training does not grow bias but grows numbers of characterizations of your thinking. #InternationalSystemsThinkingConf

I used to work with security software with risks exactly like this - possibility of taking down millions of Windows machines. This whole incident reminds me we too, decade(s) ago had problem like this that test coverage missed. But we had a few other mechanisms that protected us:

1) Delay-based distribution: the group who would get things first was small but reactive, and rendering a board member's computer useless without manual intervention did a lot of good for investments in ensuring the lessons were learned without impacting customers
2) Eating own dogfood in company: we learned to distribute internally continuously, and segment distributions. The whole environment for testing was built to provide HUMAN interventions because test systems fail.

3) Throttling, autorevert, secondary update channels: we built a number of features that would enable us to fix things without showing up face to face
4) Architectural rewrites: isolating risks like this, because not all software causes blue screens.

And then there was the continuous investment on test coverage. I am disappointed if the conclusion is that test coverage is what they missed, when they have a wealth of investments their board members would happily sponsor to never see this happen to them again.

Serendipity in action, second case with Foodora app. 

I don't want to find their bugs, but it seems I do.

Few years ago, it was one where I could get free food. Before disclosing, I worked with them to tell exactly how it reproduces, because I had managed to isolate the pattern. They fixed it, I disclosed the story, and I got slandered in infosec podcast for saying I thought I should be paid for the testing work I did. After all, that is what I do for money.

So today I am seeing another foodora bug in production, this time it steals from me. For one single order, they end up doing double withdrawal of the money. And from the authorization between three parties, I know I had to authorize it twice too. 

They tell me all I can do is wait to see if magic of systems removes the second reservation. So they can hold my money, potentially also invoice it. And all I can do is wait.

Well, I can also not use the app. I can't delete it since I need it to loop back if the magic of systems does not return my money. 

One is incidental, two is a pattern. If anyone knows folks from Foodora dev team, I offered free work on isolating it this time. But they could just also buy better testing.

Now this is fascinating: a developer on LinkedIn not only publicly corrects me on the Foodora bug being ‘by design’ but snitch tags my employer. His idea is that double reservation - which end up as money away from your use - are by design because networks are unreliable and a separate invoicing process perhaps days later removing the duplicate is how it should be. 

Holding other people’s money for days a completely reasonable impact of using online payments? Really?

Snitch-tagging tone police calling me reporting a bug "extortion". A Sunday online experience.  

Choose the right words or be silent. 

He really believes that integration with banking systems, it is a reasonable design to hold the end users money for 32+ hours in the case where there was an error in the payment flow. Assuming still the reservation does not end up as double payment, which I am not yet certain based on comparable experiences of what I see / do as user in the flow.

Applying AI in testing to do test practices that are already wasteful to do wasteful things faster is not my goal. 

For a lot of issues in testing, we have good answers that are not AI. If you don't know your coverage, observability in your application can help with that more. If 50% of your tests fail, isolating ones that pass and fixing flakiness on the rest does not need to be AI.

Two repeated patterns on how test automation fails. 
1) gym membership. Orgs fall into marketing promise of commercial tool and licenses end up on the shelf. Use beyond proof of concept does not happen. 
2) island of one. Orgs choose an open source test tool that has simplified language that developers in teams don't touch. After two or more rounds of restarts, they realize the tool needs to be chosen for team, not the individual.

I could add 3) Not Invented Here. This is when writing actual tests is considered boring and repeated, and adding features to ‘framework’ including extending pipelines with tools takes over. Most commonly spotted in test automators who aren’t contributing features and fixes in app, but also not really interested in testing.

Comparison of testing services by sampling.  They tend to get what they ask for. 

Sample 1. Resourcing responsibility. Recognizing 5 shapes of people they want to ask for: "junior" that does manual. "seasoned" that does manual+automation. "lead" for cross-team coordination. "automator" for needing more of those to ramp up automation. And "specialist" for security, performance and accessibility. 

Testing service is sending these individuals to teams in a matrix org.

Sample 2. Resourcing responsibility with an improvement twist. Someone to improve things and find people, but essentially the same as sample 1. Specific differences: extra focus on metrics, and lack of investment into automation. Everything is essentially manual.

Sample 3. Results-centric responsibility. Fairly large crowd of people but control over roles and allocations less controlled by customer. Triplication of representation through having lead + analyst + automator for everything. Automation as a service, in large batches due to unreliable environments requiring continuous analysis.

Sample 4. Automation-centric responsibility. Focused on moving automation to a helpful resource for teams through specific investment that is intended temporary. Mixed with teams having Quality-centric delivery responsibility and plan to take over all automation over time.

Coaching exploratory testing as a senior exploratory tester. Notes to self.

- No matter how they prioritize, they better have a story. That is a story of how valuable the information is, more than how much of that information there is. 

- Have better model of what could be different if you test in two environments. Understand how data and function are separate while intertwined. 

- Tell me what has not been done. I care for you recognizing work remaining more than work done.

- Stop accepting excuses. API testing is possible. Access through APIs to incoming data is possible. Prioritize for access to controls your testing needs to be valuable. 

- Stop doing as told. You need to accept the why behind what you are told because I won't accept "I was told" as a reason. In the chain of what good looks like, I will require more.

- Telling you forgot to take notes for last two weeks needs to be balanced with  what you used the time on instead. Your choice if you know why.

Reading on LinkedIn that "underperformance is always a leadership/management problem" and "the purpose of leadership/management is to get others to succeed". 

The skills gap to work with can be significant within the tester community. Investing in skilling is a clear solution. While skills are missing, underperformance is pervasive. But the idea that you will get paid a senior salary while you learn junior programmer skills does not sit well with me.

Some problems are on both sides. And decision on steps is on leadership/management.

The same heuristic is what drives me in introducing agents for exploratory testing. People can't read the walls of text, and we go a task at a time, with reflection.

The "you can take the call", and decision-avoidance. 

One of the first things I remember learning on exploratory testing is the idea that there are options, and you are making the choices. They aren't given to you with magic power of method, but you are supposed to be in control of having options. 

I presented two options today, and "you can take the call". When in fact I want us to start tracking that taking the call is equally divided, but also founded on versatile options.

As we were exploratory testing, a curious idea emerged: would the API call work if we changed order of elements. While I have no particular reason to believe that the order of elements makes a difference, we embraced the curiosity and tried it. Concluded it did not matter. 

What makes me wonder though is that the same point of curiosity was then applied on every field. Setting up an experiment where the scope is not "everything" was harder than I realized.

Teaching #ContemporaryExploratoryTesting with AI today. 

What we did: 
- Started with a repo with application code
- Tested remote control by creating list of participants while doing introductions
- Generated a list of features by access to code
- Generated a list of bugs (11) by access to code
- Installed playwright and playwright agents
- Generated a list of bugs (21) by access to the UI

- Combined the two lists of bugs to identify overlap
- Generated test cases with playwright agents
- Compared the list of features to test cases for coverage analysis
- Automated a failing test for bug number 3
- Fixed the bug by requesting a fix for bug number 3
- Run the test automation to see it passing
- Refactored the automated tests to POM

Looks like there is (at least) three layers of testing for this AI upgrade of 1M lines of Java code, and new team-level vocabulary to talk about it. 

The *generator tests* are systematically generated with AI on a recipe that includes example tests driven by code coverage and property based testing. 

The *behavior tests* are existing test base. They risk needing to change in ways that we can't quite control, but they hold our past truth. 

The *prod playback tests* are our new approach on the risks of change we can't even pinpoint. 

And we need to add *future maintenance assessment* because we'll live with what we leave behind.
